subject: geography
book: Fundamentals of Human Geography; India: People and Economy (NCERT, rationalised) [practical: Practical Work in Geography Part II]

chapters.title: Human: Human Geography: Nature and Scope

sections.name: 1.1 Introduction: geography as an integrating discipline

concepts.text: Geography as a field of study is integrative, empirical and practical; studies phenomena varying over space and time
Dualism in geography: physical geography vs human geography; recap of Class 11 branches
Human geography studies the interrelationship between the physical environment and socio-cultural environment created by humans
Ratzel: human geography is the synthetic study of relationship between human societies and earth's surface
Ellen C. Semple: human geography is the study of the changing relationship between unresting man and unstable earth
Paul Vidal de la Blache: conception resulting from more synthetic knowledge of physical laws governing earth and relations between living beings
Common theme: relationship between humans and the environment is dynamic
Elements of physical environment: landforms, soils, climate, water, natural vegetation, flora and fauna
Elements of cultural landscape created by humans: houses, villages, cities, road-rail networks, industries, farms, ports, items of daily use
Humans use technology to interact with environment; technology indicates level of cultural development
Human activities shape cultural landscape on the physical environment

sections.name: 1.4 Naturalisation of humans and humanisation of nature

concepts.text: Interaction between primitive societies and nature: environmental determinism; example of Benda in Abujh Marh (Central India) depending on nature
Nature as 'Mother Nature' - fear, worship; naturalisation of humans
Humanisation of nature: with technology humans create possibilities - possibilism; example of Trondheim (Norway) in winter with technology
Imprints of human activities: health resorts on highlands, urban sprawls, orchards, pastures, ports, oceanic routes, satellites in space
Neo-determinism (stop and go determinism) by Griffith Taylor: middle path - humans follow nature's signals like traffic lights; limits to development
Comparison of environmental determinism, possibilism and neo-determinism

sections.name: 1.5 Human geography through the corridors of time

concepts.text: Early colonial period: exploration and description; imperial and trade interests; travel accounts
Later colonial period: regional analysis - elaborate description of all aspects of a region (part to whole)
1930s inter-war period: areal differentiation - why and how regions differ (Hartshorne)
Late 1950s to late 1960s: spatial organisation - quantitative revolution, use of computers and statistical tools, laws and spatial patterns
1970s: emergence of humanistic, radical and behavioural schools - dissatisfaction with quantitative approach
Humanistic geography: central role of human awareness, agency, consciousness and creativity
Radical (welfare) school: Marxian theory to explain poverty, deprivation and social inequality
Behavioural school: lived experience, perception of space by social categories (ethnicity, race, religion)
1990s: post-modernism - questioning grand generalisations; importance of local context
Table type: broad stages and thrust of human geography in chronological order

sections.name: 1.6 Fields and sub-fields of human geography

concepts.text: Human geography is interdisciplinary with close links to sister disciplines in social sciences
Social geography: behavioural geography, geography of social well-being, geography of leisure, cultural geography, gender geography, historical geography, medical geography
Urban geography linked with urban studies and planning
Political geography: electoral geography, military geography (links with political science, military science)
Population geography linked with demography; settlement geography with urban and rural planning

Economic geography: geography of resources, agriculture, industry, marketing, tourism, international trade (links with economics, agricultural sciences, industrial economics, business studies, tourism)
Table type: human geography and sister disciplines of social sciences
Exercise types: MCQs on definitions and schools; distinguish naturalisation of humans and humanisation of nature; describe nature/scope; explain neo-determinism; describe fields and sub-fields

chapters.title: Human: The World Population: Distribution, Density and Growth

concepts.text: People of a country are its real wealth; resources are used by them and policies made by them
World population more than 8 billion (7.9 billion in 2021 text figure); growth over centuries
Population studied in terms of distribution, density, growth and composition

sections.name: 2.2 Patterns of population distribution in the world

concepts.text: Distribution: way people are spaced over earth's surface
Broadly, 90 percent of world population lives in about 10 percent of land area
10 most populous countries contribute about 60 percent of world population; 6 of these in Asia
Map reading: world distribution of population - densely, moderately, sparsely populated areas
Density: ratio between number of people and size of land, in persons per sq km
Formula: density = population / area; worked numerical example (e.g. 1,50,000 people on 100 sq km = 1,500 per sq km)
Densely populated regions: north-eastern USA, north-western Europe, South, South-east and East Asia
Sparsely populated areas: near poles, high rainfall zones near equator, hot and cold deserts
Medium density areas: western China, southern India, Norway, Sweden

sections.name: 2.4 Factors influencing the distribution of population

concepts.text: Geographical factors: availability of water (river valleys most densely populated)
Landforms: flat plains and gentle slopes preferred (Ganga plains vs Andes, Alps, Himalayas)
Climate: extreme climates (hot/cold deserts) discourage settlement; comfortable climate (Mediterranean) attracts
Soils: fertile loamy soils support intensive agriculture (Nile, Ganga, Hwang-He, Chang Jiang plains)
Economic factors: minerals attract industries and people (Katanga Zambia copper belt, Karnataka gold)
Urbanisation: better civic amenities, employment, education, medical facilities attract rural-urban migrants
Industrialisation: industrial belts attract labour (Kobe-Osaka region of Japan)
Social and cultural factors: religious or cultural significance (Varanasi, Jerusalem, Vatican City); social and political unrest causes outmigration; tax incentives attract people
Population growth/change: change in number of inhabitants over time, positive or negative
Growth of population: change in population between two points of time (absolute numbers)
Growth rate of population: change expressed as percentage
Natural growth of population: increase by difference between births and deaths
Actual growth of population: births - deaths + in-migration - out-migration
Positive growth (births exceed deaths or immigration) and negative growth (population decreases)
Worked numerical type: compute growth and growth rate from two census figures
Three components: births, deaths and migration
Crude Birth Rate (CBR): number of live births in a year per thousand of population; formula CBR = Bi/P x 1000
Crude Death Rate (CDR): number of deaths in a year per thousand of population; formula CDR = D/P x 1000
Factors affecting mortality: demographic structure, social advancement, economic development
Migration: change of place of residence; place of origin and place of destination; immigrants and emigrants
Permanent, temporary or seasonal migration; rural-rural, rural-urban, urban-urban, urban-rural
Push factors (unemployment, poor living conditions, political turmoil, unpleasant climate, natural disasters, epidemics, socio-economic backwardness)
Pull factors (better jobs, living conditions, peace and stability, security of life and property, pleasant climate)
Population grew slowly in early periods; rapid growth after industrial revolution (about 1750)
Population was 0.3 billion around first century AD; 1 billion around 1820s; then doubled rapidly
Technological advancement, Industrial Revolution, medical facilities and improved food supply reduced death rate
Doubling time of world population: periods taken to double shrinking over time
Table type: doubling time of world population; graph of population growth through history
Spatial pattern of population growth: developed countries slower; developing countries faster; negative growth in some countries
Small increase desirable for growing economy; beyond a point it creates problems
Problems of rapid growth: depletion of resources, unemployment, pressure on services
Problems of population decline: resources underutilised; ageing; shrinking workforce
Demographic transition theory: population shifts from high births and deaths to low births and deaths as society progresses from rural agrarian illiterate to urban industrial literate
Stage I: high fertility and high mortality; slow growth; agriculture, low life expectancy, mostly illiterate
Stage II: fertility remains high initially then declines; mortality reduces due to better sanitation and health; large increase in population
Stage III: both fertility and mortality decline considerably; population stable or grows slowly; urbanised, literate, high technical know-how
Diagram type: demographic transition model with birth rate, death rate and total population curves
Examples of countries at different stages
Family planning: spacing or preventing birth of children; access to family planning services
Government role: propaganda, free availability of contraceptives, tax disincentives for large families
Thomas Malthus' theory (1798): population grows faster than food supply leading to famine, disease and war (natural checks)
Preventive checks vs natural checks in Malthusian theory
Exercise types: MCQs on distribution, demographic transition; three geographical factors; positive vs negative growth; explain demographic transition theory; factors influencing distribution
Growth and development both refer to changes over time
Growth is quantitative and value neutral - positive or negative
Development is qualitative change and always value positive; growth plus positive change in quality
Earlier, development measured by economic growth only; GNP, per capita income
Paradox: high economic growth can coexist with poor human development
Introduced by Dr Mahbub-ul-Haq (Pakistani economist): development that enlarges people's choices and improves lives; people central
Prof. Amartya Sen: expansion of freedom (decrease of unfreedom) as main objective of development; role of social and political institutions
Human Development Report published by UNDP since 1990
Leading a long and healthy life, being able to gain knowledge and having enough means to live a decent life are most important aspects
Access to resources, health and education as key areas; lack of capabilities limits choices
Equity: making equal access to opportunities available to everybody irrespective of gender, race, income, caste
Example: dropout rates among women and socially/economically backward groups in India
Sustainability: continuity in availability of opportunities for future generations; misuse of resources reduces options
Productivity: human labour productivity; enriching capabilities via investment in people (people as real wealth of nations)
Empowerment: having the power to make choices; good governance and people-oriented policies; empowerment of socially and economically disadvantaged groups
Income approach: oldest; human development linked to income; higher income means higher level
Welfare approach: humans as beneficiaries of development; government spending on education, health, social amenities; people passive recipients
Basic needs approach: initially proposed by International Labour Organisation (ILO); six basic needs - health, education, food, water supply, sanitation and housing; human choices ignored
Capability approach: associated with Prof. Amartya Sen; building human capabilities in health, education and access to resources is key
Table/comparison: four approaches and their emphasis
Human Development Index (HDI): ranks countries based on performance in health, education and access to resources; scores 0 to 1
Health indicator: life expectancy at birth; longer life expectancy indicates healthy life
Education indicator: adult literacy rate and gross enrolment ratio (mean years of schooling and expected years of schooling)
Access to resources: purchasing power (in US dollars; GNI per capita PPP)
Each dimension given weightage of 1/3; HDI as sum of weights
HDI measures attainment; Human Poverty Index (HPI) measures shortfall - probability of not surviving to 40, adult illiteracy, number without access to clean water, small underweight children
Other indices: Gross National Happiness (Bhutan) - measures country's progress by happiness; spiritual, non-material and qualitative aspects
Worked task type: interpret HDI scores and ranks
Size of territory and per capita income not directly related to human development (small countries may do better than large ones)
Countries grouped into four categories by HDI score: very high (above 0.800), high (0.700-0.799), medium (0.550-0.699), low (below 0.549)
Very high and high HDI countries: invest more in social sector, free of political turmoil; e.g. Norway, Switzerland, Australia
Medium HDI countries: mostly emerged after colonial period; trying to improve; diversity in population; India in this group
Low HDI countries: small countries with political turmoil, civil war, famine, high incidence of diseases; e.g. sub-Saharan Africa
Role of governance and social sector spending in human development
Map reading: world HDI categories; table of top and bottom countries
Exercise types: MCQs on pillars and approaches; differentiate growth and development; explain the four pillars; key areas of human development; HDI categories and characteristics
Economic activities: primary, secondary, tertiary, quaternary and quinary
Primary activities directly dependent on environment: hunting, gathering, pastoral activities, fishing, forestry, agriculture, mining and quarrying
Red-collar workers: people engaged in primary activities (outdoor work)
Proportion of workforce in primary sector falls as economies develop
Earliest human activities: dependence on environment for food, shelter, clothing
Hunting with primitive tools - stones, twigs, arrows; fishing in coastal areas
Gathering practised in high latitudes (northern Canada, northern Eurasia, southern Chile) and low latitudes (Amazon basin, tropical Africa, northern Australia, South-east Asia interiors)
Modern gathering is market-oriented: valuable plants and leaves, bark (quinine, tannin), fibre, gums, resins; chicle (chewing gum)
Low capital/skill investment and low yield per person; no surplus
Map work: areas of subsistence gathering on world map
Animal domestication followed hunting; pastoralism as subsistence or commercial
Nomadic herding (pastoral nomadism): primitive subsistence activity depending on animals for food, clothing, shelter, tools and transport
Animals by region: cattle in tropical Africa; sheep, goats, camels in Sahara and Asian deserts; yak in Tibet; llamas in Andes; reindeer in Arctic and sub-Arctic

Three important regions of nomadic herding: core region from Atlantic shores of North Africa eastwards across Arabian peninsula into Mongolia and Central China; tundra region of Eurasia; south-west Africa and Madagascar
Transhumance: seasonal migration of herders; e.g. Gujjars, Bakarwals, Gaddis and Bhotiyas move from plains to mountains in summer and back in winter
Decline of pastoral nomadism due to political boundaries and new settlement plans
Map work: areas of nomadic herding
More organised and capital intensive; practised on permanent ranches
Ranches: large areas divided into parcels fenced to regulate grazing; rotational grazing
Specialised activity rearing one type of animal: sheep, cattle, goats, horses; products processed and packed scientifically for world markets
Scientific breeding, genetic improvement, disease control and healthcare
Important in New Zealand, Australia, Argentina, Uruguay and USA
Map work: areas of commercial livestock rearing
Agriculture practised under multiple combinations of physical and socio-economic conditions
Subsistence agriculture: farmers consume all or nearly all produce
Primitive subsistence agriculture (shifting cultivation/slash and burn): tropical Africa, South and Central America, South-east Asia
Shifting cultivation: vegetation cleared by fire, ashes add to fertility; cultivated for 3-5 years then abandoned; cycle of jhumming shortens with population
Regional names: Jhuming in north-eastern India, Milpa in Central America and Mexico, Ladang in Indonesia and Malaysia
Intensive subsistence agriculture: densely populated monsoon Asia
Intensive subsistence agriculture dominated by wet paddy: small holdings, family labour, intensive use of land, manure; high yield per unit area, low labour productivity
Intensive subsistence agriculture dominated by crops other than paddy: wheat, soyabean, barley, sorghum in northern China, Manchuria, North Korea, North Japan; irrigation used
Introduced by Europeans in colonies in tropics
Crops: tea, coffee, cocoa, rubber, cotton, oil palm, sugarcane, bananas, pineapples

Characteristics: large estates, large capital investment, managerial and technical support, scientific methods, single crop specialisation, cheap labour, good transport linking estates to factories and markets

Examples: French cocoa and coffee in West Africa, British tea gardens in India and Sri Lanka, rubber in Malaysia, sugarcane and bananas in West Indies; Spanish and Americans in coconut and sugarcane in Philippines; Dutch sugarcane in Indonesia
Some plantations now owned by governments or nationals of the countries
Practised in interior parts of semi-arid lands of mid-latitudes
Wheat as principal crop; also corn, barley, oats, rye
Very large farms (240-16,000 hectares); highly mechanised; low yield per acre but high yield per person
Regions: Eurasian steppes, Canadian and American Prairies, Pampas of Argentina, Velds of South Africa, Australian Downs, Canterbury Plains of New Zealand
Map work: areas of extensive commercial grain farming
Found in highly developed parts of world: north-western Europe, eastern North America, parts of Eurasia, temperate latitudes of southern continents
Moderate-sized farms; crops - wheat, barley, oats, rye, maize, fodder and root crops
Fodder crops important; crop rotation and intercropping maintain fertility
Equal emphasis on crop cultivation and animal husbandry (cattle, sheep, pigs, poultry)
High capital expenditure on machinery and buildings, extensive use of fertilisers and green manures; skill and expertise of farmers
Map work: areas of mixed farming
Most advanced and efficient type of rearing milch animals
Highly capital intensive: animal sheds, storage for fodder, feeding and milking machines; veterinary services
Highly labour intensive - rigorous care in feeding and milking; no off-season
Practised near urban and industrial centres for fresh milk and dairy products; refrigeration, pasteurisation and preservation increased storage
Three main regions: north-western Europe (largest), Canada, and south-eastern Australia, New Zealand and Tasmania
Highly specialised commercial agriculture in countries on either side of Mediterranean Sea, California, central Chile, south-western South Africa and south-western Australia
Important supplier of citrus fruits
Viticulture (grape cultivation) is a speciality; best quality wines; inferior grapes dried into raisins and currants; olives and figs
Advantage: winter supply of fruits and vegetables to European and North American markets
Cultivation of high value crops - vegetables, fruits and flowers - for urban markets
Small farms near good transport links to urban centres; labour and capital intensive; irrigation, HYV seeds, fertilisers, insecticides, greenhouses and artificial heating
Well developed in densely populated industrial districts of north-west Europe, north-eastern USA and Mediterranean; Netherlands specialises in flowers (tulips) flown to major European cities
Truck farming: regions specialising in vegetables only; distance a truck can cover overnight determines the area
Factory farming: modern development in western Europe and North America; livestock (poultry, cattle) reared in stalls and pens, fed on manufactured feed; capital intensive
Classification of farming by organisation: ownership by farmers, government or cooperative
Cooperative farming: farmers pool resources voluntarily for more efficient and profitable farming; cooperative societies help in procuring inputs, selling products, processing
Successful in Denmark, Netherlands, Belgium, Sweden, Italy; Denmark - every farmer is a member of a cooperative
Collective farming (Kolkhoz): based on social ownership of means of production and collective labour; introduced in erstwhile Soviet Union
Collective farming: farmers pool resources, retain small plots for own use; government fixes targets and buys produce at fixed prices; surplus distributed among members; later modified
Mining as primary activity; Copper age and Bronze age reflect importance of minerals in history
Factors affecting mining: physical factors - size, grade and mode of occurrence of deposits
Economic factors: demand for mineral, technology available, capital to develop infrastructure, labour and transport costs
Methods of mining: surface (open-cast) mining - easiest and cheapest for minerals near surface; low safety precautions and equipment cost, fast output
Underground (shaft) mining: for deep deposits; vertical shafts, underground galleries; needs lifts, drills, haulage vehicles, ventilation; risky (poisonous gases, fires, floods, caving in)
Developed vs developing economies: developed countries retreating from mining due to high labour costs; developing countries depend on mineral exports

Exercise types: MCQs on farming types and regions; differentiate nomadic herding vs commercial livestock rearing; plantation characteristics; shifting cultivation problems; mixed farming and dairy farming; factors affecting mining; map identification
Secondary activities add value to natural resources by transforming raw materials into valuable products
Includes manufacturing, processing and construction (infrastructure) industries
Example: cotton to yarn to fabric; iron ore to steel
Manufacturing: production of goods from raw materials; from handicrafts to moulding iron and steel, to space vehicles
Literal meaning 'to make by hand'; now includes goods made by machines
Essential features: application of power, mass production of identical products, specialised labour in factory settings
Manufacturing vs industry: industry is broader term (e.g. tourism industry); manufacturing is subset
Blue-collar workers in manufacturing

sections.name: 5.3 Characteristics of modern large scale manufacturing

concepts.text: Specialisation of skills/methods of production: craft method makes few custom pieces; mass production makes large quantities of standard parts with each worker doing one task
Mechanisation: using machines; automation - advanced stage without human thinking; feedback and closed-loop computer control systems
Technological innovation: research and development for quality control, eliminating waste and inefficiency, combating pollution
Organisational structure and stratification: complex machine technology; extreme specialisation and division of labour; vast capital; large organisations; executive bureaucracy
Uneven geographic distribution: major concentrations in less than 10 percent of world's land area; power centres of economic and political power
Industries maximise profits by cutting costs; located where production costs are lowest
Access to market: most important factor; developed regions with large purchasing power; densely populated developing regions; some industries serve global markets (aircraft, arms)
Access to raw material: cheap and easily transported; weight-losing materials located near raw material (steel, sugar, cement, dairy); perishables near source
Access to labour: mechanisation reduced labour need, but some industries need skilled labour
Access to sources of energy: industries using more power located near energy sources (aluminium industry); hydroelectricity
Access to transportation and communication facilities: speedy and efficient transport for raw materials and finished goods; Western Europe and eastern North America examples
Government policy: regional policies promoting balanced economic development; incentives for backward areas
Access to agglomeration economies/links between industries: benefits from proximity to leader industry and other industries
Footloose industries can be located anywhere; not dependent on any specific raw material, weight losing or not
Depend on component parts obtainable anywhere; produce in small quantity; employ small labour force; generally non-polluting
Important factor: accessibility by road network (e.g. diamonds, computer chips, mobile manufacturing)

sections.name: 5.6 Classification of manufacturing industries: by size

concepts.text: Bases of classification: size, inputs/raw materials, output/products, ownership
Household industries or cottage manufacturing: smallest unit; artisans with family members using local materials and simple tools; products for local market (pottery, basket weaving, handicrafts)
Small scale manufacturing: workshop outside home; local raw materials, simple power-driven machines and semi-skilled labour; employment generation (India, China, Indonesia, Brazil)
Large scale manufacturing: large market, various raw materials, enormous energy, specialised workers, advanced technology, assembly-line mass production, large capital
Large scale manufacturing regions: Great Lakes region of USA, Western Europe, Eastern Europe, Japan; also Brazil, China, India, South Korea etc.

Agro-based industries: processing raw materials from fields and farms - food processing, sugar, pickles, fruit juices, beverages (tea, coffee, cocoa), spices, oils, textiles (cotton, jute, silk), rubber
Food processing: canning, producing cream, fruit processing, confectionery; agri-business - commercial farming on industrial scale financed by business
Mineral based industries: ferrous metallic minerals (iron and steel), non-ferrous (aluminium, copper, jewellery); non-metallic minerals (cement, pottery)
Chemical based industries: natural chemical minerals (coal, petroleum, salts, sulphur, potash); petro-chemicals; synthetic fibres, plastics
Forest based raw material industries: timber for furniture, wood pulp for paper; lac, gums, resins
Animal based industries: leather industry (hides and skins), woollen textiles (wool), ivory (elephant tusks)

sections.name: 5.8 Classification by output/product and by ownership

concepts.text: Basic industries: products used to make other goods (iron and steel to machinery)
Consumer goods industries: produce goods consumed directly (bread, biscuits, tea, soaps, toiletries, paper, TVs)
Public sector industries: owned and managed by government; many in socialist countries; mixed economies
Private sector industries: owned by individual investors or private organisations; capitalist countries
Joint sector industries: managed by joint stock companies or private and public sector together
High technology (high-tech): latest generation of manufacturing; intensive research and development (R and D) leading to advanced scientific and engineering products
Professional (white collar) workers form large share of workforce
Robotics on assembly lines, computer-aided design (CAD) and manufacturing, electronic controls of smelting and refining, new chemical and pharmaceutical products
Neatly spaced, low, modern dispersed office-plant-lab buildings rather than massive assembly structures; planned business parks
Technopolis: regional and local technology concentrations; Silicon Valley near San Francisco and Silicon Forest near Seattle as examples
Manufacturing contributes significantly to world economy; iron and steel, textiles, automobiles, petrochemicals, electronics
Exercise types: MCQs on footloose, agro-based, high-tech; characteristics of modern manufacturing; locational factors; classification of industries; what is high-tech industry
Tertiary activities related to service sector: professional services (health, education, law, governance) and recreation
Manpower an important component; skilled workers; output in terms of services not tangible goods
Difference between secondary and tertiary: expertise via specialised skills/experience vs production techniques and machinery
Exchange of goods and services; in developed countries majority of workers employed in tertiary sector
Tertiary activities include trade, transport, communication and services
Trade and commerce, transport and communication, services (government, private), tourism
Services provided at different levels: some to industries, some to people, some to both
Trade: buying and selling of items produced elsewhere; services in retail and wholesale trade or commerce
Trading centres: rural marketing centres and urban marketing centres
Rural marketing centres: cater to nearby settlements; quasi-urban centres; personal and professional services not well developed
Periodic markets: in rural areas where regular markets absent; weekly, bi-weekly markets; held at fixed intervals (haats)

Urban marketing centres: more specialised services; ordinary goods and specialised goods/services; labour markets, housing, semi/finished products, services of educational institutions and professionals (doctors, lawyers, teachers)
Retail trading: sale of goods directly to consumers; stores, departmental stores, chain stores, street peddling, handcarts, mail order, telephone, internet, automatic vending
Consumer cooperatives - first in large-scale innovations; departmental stores; chain stores
Wholesale trading: through intermediary merchants and supply houses; supply to retail stores; credit to retail stores
Transport: service by which persons, manufactured goods and property are physically carried from one location to another
Organised industry created to satisfy basic need of mobility
Transport distance measured as km distance (route length), time distance and cost distance
Network: nodes (meeting points of two or more routes) and links (roads joining nodes)

Factors affecting transport services: demand for transport (population size), routes - cities, towns, villages, industrial centres, raw materials, pattern of trade, nature of landscape, climate, funds
Communication services: transmission of words, messages, facts and ideas
Early communication by drums, smoke signals, runners and animals; writing preserved messages
Telecommunications: telegraph, telephone, cellular phones; satellites and internet; fibre optic cables; instantaneous transmission
Mass media: radio and television for news, entertainment and advertising; newspapers
Services occur at different levels: industry, people, both (e.g. transport system)
Low-order services (grocery, laundry) more common than high-order services (accountants, consultants, physicians)
Services provided by government or companies; public utilities - water, electricity; transport and communication
Business services: advertising, legal services, public relations, consultancy
Personal services: workers who migrate to cities for livelihood - housekeepers, cooks, gardeners; unorganised sector
People engaged in tertiary activities: growing share of workforce in developed countries (over 75 percent in USA); rising in developing countries
Tourism: travel undertaken for recreation rather than business; world's single largest tertiary activity in total registered jobs (250 million) and revenue
Tourism fosters growth of infrastructure, retail trading and craft industries (souvenirs)
Tourism seasons: vacations, holiday seasons; Mediterranean coast and west coast of India popular destinations

Tourist attractions: climate (warm sunny beaches, winter sports), landscape (mountains, lakes, sea coasts), history and art (ancient or picturesque towns, archaeological sites), culture and economy (ethnic and local customs, home stays)
Tourist regions: warmer places around Mediterranean coast and west coast of India; winter sports in mountainous areas
Medical tourism: international patients travel to India for affordable medical treatment (Apollo, Fortis etc.); outsourcing medical tests and data interpretation
Quaternary activities: knowledge-based - collection, production and dissemination of information; research and development
Examples: services in finance, banking, insurance, consultancy, software development, research, education (teachers, librarians), data processing
Quaternary workers called white-collar knowledge workers; not tied to resources or market location
Quaternary sector growing rapidly in developed economies; workforce shift from primary to quaternary over time
Quinary activities: services focusing on creation, rearrangement, interpretation of new and existing ideas; data interpretation, new technologies
Gold collar professions: highest decision makers or policy makers - senior executives, government officials, research scientists, financial and legal consultants
Highly paid skills and special knowledge; importance in post-industrial economies
Outsourcing (contracting out): giving work to an outside agency to improve efficiency and reduce costs
Offshoring: outsourcing involving transfer of work to overseas locations
Business Process Outsourcing (BPO): IT-enabled services, call centres, data processing; India, China, Eastern Europe, Israel, Philippines, Costa Rica as destinations
Knowledge Processing Outsourcing (KPO): high-skilled information-driven knowledge outsourcing - R and D, e-learning, business research, intellectual property research, legal profession, banking
Home-shoring: alternative to outsourcing; digital divide - uneven access to ICT between and within countries
Benefits and concerns of outsourcing for countries; need for skilled labour

Exercise types: MCQs on tertiary/quaternary/quinary examples; differentiate tertiary and secondary; periodic markets; retail vs wholesale; tourism factors; medical tourism; outsourcing and digital divide
Transport and communication bridge spatial gaps between production and consumption
Transport: service or facility for carriage of people and goods; three basic modes - land, water and air; also pipelines and cables
Choice of mode depends on cost of transport, type of goods, distance, urgency
Transport network: nodes and links; transport as an industry
Land transport: pack animals, carts, roads, railways; human porters in hilly regions
Mode selection: cost and time considerations; long distances by ships/air, short distances by road
Intermodal and containerisation: integrating different modes for efficiency
Water and air transport complement land transport; pipelines for fluids
Roads most economical for short distances; door-to-door service; flexible
Quality of roads varies; metalled (all-weather) vs unmetalled roads; problems of seasonal roads in monsoon
World total motorable road length about 15 million km; North America has highest road density
Traffic flows and congestion in cities; peak hours; urban transport problems

Highways: metalled roads connecting distant places; four-lane or more; e.g. Trans-Canadian Highway, Alaskan Highway, Pan-American Highway, Trans-Continental Stuart Highway (Australia), Indian National Highways (Golden Quadrilateral)
Border roads: roads along international boundaries; integrate remote areas; Border Roads Organisation in India
Road density and road network map reading
Railways: mode for bulky goods and passengers over long distances; gauges differ (broad, standard, metre, narrow)
Commuter trains important in cities like London, Paris, Tokyo, Mumbai
Rail network densest in Europe; around 1.3 million km of railways in world; also North America (USA, Canada), Australia
Trans-continental railways: run across continent linking its two ends
Trans-Siberian railway: St Petersburg in west to Vladivostok on Pacific coast; 9,332 km; double-tracked and electrified; most important route in Asia
Trans-Canadian railway: Halifax in east to Vancouver on Pacific coast; 7,050 km; passes Montreal, Ottawa, Winnipeg, Calgary; wheat belt and coniferous forests
Union and Pacific railway: New York on Atlantic coast to San Francisco on Pacific
Australian trans-continental railway: Perth on west coast to Sydney on east coast across Nullabor Plains
Orient Express: Paris to Istanbul via Strasbourg, Munich, Vienna, Budapest, Belgrade
Map work: terminal stations of transcontinental railways
Advantage: no route construction needed; oceans linked; cheapest for bulky goods over long distances; energy efficient
Modern passenger liners and cargo ships with radar, wireless, navigation aids; refrigerated chambers; container ships; specialised ports
Northern Atlantic sea route: links north-eastern USA and north-western Europe; 'Big Trunk route'; one-fourth of world trade
Mediterranean-Indian Ocean sea route (via Suez canal): links Western Europe with West Africa, South Africa, South-east Asia, Australia and New Zealand
Cape of Good Hope sea route: links west European and west African countries with Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay
Southern Atlantic sea route: across South Atlantic linking South America and Africa
North Pacific sea route: links western coast of North America with Asia; Vancouver, Seattle, Portland, San Francisco, Los Angeles with Yokohama, Kobe, Shanghai, Hong Kong, Manila, Singapore
South Pacific sea route: links Western Europe and North America with Australia, New Zealand and Pacific islands via Panama canal
Coastal shipping: convenient mode for countries with long coastlines (USA, China, India); reduces road congestion

Suez Canal: constructed 1869 in Egypt between Port Said (north) and Port Suez (south) linking Mediterranean and Red Sea; sea-level canal without locks; about 160 km long; gives Europe a new gateway to Indian Ocean
Panama Canal: connects Atlantic Ocean in east to Pacific in west; built by US government; about 72 km long; six lock systems; shortens distance between New York and San Francisco by 13,000 km
Comparison between Suez and Panama canals (locks, length, trade importance)
Rivers, canals, lakes and coastal areas as inland waterways; boats and steamers
Development depends on navigability, width and depth of channel, continuity of water flow, technology
Rhine waterway: through Germany and Netherlands; navigable 700 km from Rotterdam to Basel in Switzerland; Ruhr coalfield; heavily used waterway in world
Danube waterway: serves Eastern Europe; rises in Black Forest; navigable up to Taurna Severin; exports wheat, maize, timber, machinery
Volga waterway: Russia's most important; navigable for 11,200 km; drains into Caspian Sea; Volga-Moscow canal and Volga-Don canal
Great Lakes-St. Lawrence seaway: Superior, Huron, Erie, Ontario connected by Soo canal and Welland canal; St Lawrence estuary; important for North America
Mississippi waterways: connects Great Lakes with Gulf of Mexico; large steamers up to Minneapolis
Map work: important inland waterways
Fastest mode of transport but very costly; suitable for high-value, light and perishable goods
Accessibility to remote and inaccessible areas (mountains, snowfields, deserts); helicopters in hilly areas
Air transport crucial during emergencies: rescue, relief
Manufacture of aircraft and operation of air transport require huge infrastructure and investment
Inter-continental air routes: dense network in Northern hemisphere - eastern USA, Western Europe and South-east Asia; USA alone accounts for about 60 percent of air routes
Southern hemisphere has limited air services due to sparse population, small landmass and economic development
Map work: major airports of the world
Pipelines used to transport liquids and gases - water, petroleum, natural gas; also liquefied coal
Big Inch pipeline in USA carries petroleum from oil wells of Gulf of Mexico to north-eastern states
Pipelines from oil fields to ports and refineries in Europe, Russia, West Asia; Iran-Oman-India gas pipeline proposal, Iran-Pakistan-India (IPI) proposals
Advantages: continuous supply, low running cost, less loss; disadvantages: high construction cost, leakages difficult to detect
Communication: transfer of messages over distance; long-distance communication earlier by land/sea; invention of telegraph and telephone
Telecommunications: speed of transmission; telegraph to telephone to cellular phones; fibre optic cables (large data, speedy, secure)
Satellite communication: since 1970s; Indian satellites (Aryabhatta 1975, Bhaskar, Rohini; INSAT series)
Cyberspace and the internet: electronic digital world of computers; World Wide Web; expansion of internet users worldwide
Internet as information superhighway; e-commerce, e-governance, e-learning; changes in social and economic life

Exercise types: MCQs on trans-continental railways, sea routes and canals; advantages of water transport; importance of pipelines; air transport significance; satellite communication and cyberspace; map identification of terminals, seaports, airports, waterways
Trade: voluntary exchange of goods and services; requires two parties
International trade: exchange of goods and services among countries across national boundaries
Need for trade: countries cannot produce everything; specialisation
Barter system: direct exchange of goods; difficulties of double coincidence of wants
Jon Beel Mela in Jagiroad (Assam) after harvest - barter still practised
Introduction of money as medium of exchange solved barter difficulties
Silk Route: early example of long-distance trade connecting Rome to China (6,000 km); silk, wool, metals
After fall of Roman empire: European commerce in 12th and 13th centuries; ocean-going warships; trade between Europe and Asia; discovery of Americas
Slave trade (15th century onwards): Portuguese, Dutch, Spanish and British captured Africans for plantations in Americas; abolished in Denmark (1792), Great Britain (1807), USA (1808)
After industrial revolution: raw materials from colonies and manufactured goods from industrialised nations
During World Wars: trade taxes and quantitative restrictions; post-war General Agreement for Tariffs and Trade (GATT) to reduce tariffs
Pattern of trade shaped by colonialism and later globalisation
Difference in national resources: unequal distribution of world resources
Geological structure: determines mineral resource base; topographic differences ensure diversity of crops and animals
Mineral resources unevenly distributed; availability of mineral resources provides basis for industrial development
Climate: influences type of flora and fauna (wool in cold regions; bananas, rubber, cocoa in tropics)
Population factors: cultural factors (distinctive art and crafts - China porcelain, Iran carpets, Indonesian batik); size of population (densely populated have large internal trade)
Stage of economic development: agricultural countries export agro products, import manufactured goods; industrial countries export machinery
Extent of foreign investment: boosts trade in developing countries lacking capital (mining, oil drilling, plantations)
Transport: expansion of rail, ocean and air transport, refrigeration and preservation improved trade
Volume of trade: actual tonnage of goods traded; measured by total value of goods and services
Composition of trade: nature of goods and services imported and exported; shift from primary products to manufactured goods and services
Direction of trade: historically developing countries exported raw materials; trend changing - Asian countries (China, India) now major partners
Balance of trade: record of volume of goods and services imported and exported
Positive (favourable) balance of trade: exports exceed imports; negative (unfavourable) when imports exceed exports
Negative balance means spending more on buying than selling, leading to exhaustion of financial reserves
Balance of payments as a broader concept including services and capital flows
Bilateral trade: trade by two countries with each other based on agreed commodities
Multilateral trade: trade with many countries; granting most favoured nation (MFN) status to some partners
Free trade or trade liberalisation: opening economies for trade by lowering trade barriers like tariffs
Liberalisation allows goods and services to compete with domestic products
Globalisation and free trade can adversely affect economies of developing countries by uneven playing field
Dumping: selling a commodity in another country at a price lower than its cost and below domestic price; need to protect against dumped goods
GATT formed in 1948 to liberalise world from high customs tariffs and other restrictions
WTO set up on 1 January 1995 as permanent institution; headquarters in Geneva, Switzerland
WTO sets rules for global trading system and resolves disputes between member nations
Covers trade in services (telecommunication, banking) and intellectual property rights
Criticism: free trade does not make people more prosperous; widens gap between rich and poor; neglects environment, health, worker rights; dominance of developed countries
India as a founder member of WTO
Regional trade blocs encourage trade among countries with geographical proximity, similarity and complementarity in trading items; curb restrictions
About 120 regional trade blocs generate 52 percent of world trade
ASEAN (Association of South-East Asian Nations): headquarters Jakarta; formed 1967; agro products, rubber, palm oil, rice, copra, coffee, minerals
CIS (Commonwealth of Independent States): headquarters Minsk; formed 1991; crude oil, natural gas, gold, cotton, fibre
EU (European Union): headquarters Brussels; formed 1957 as EEC, EU in 1992; single market, common currency (euro); agro products, minerals, chemicals, wood, vehicles, transport equipment
LAIA (Latin American Integration Association): headquarters Montevideo, Uruguay; formed 1960
NAFTA (North American Free Trade Association): USA, Canada, Mexico; formed 1994 (replaced by USMCA in 2020)
OPEC (Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries): headquarters Vienna; formed 1949/1960; crude petroleum
SAFTA (South Asian Free Trade Agreement): SAARC countries; formed January 2006; reduce tariffs on intra-regional trade
Table type: regional trade blocs with headquarters, member countries, origin, commodities
Mutually beneficial if it leads to regional specialisation, higher production, better standard of living and access to goods
Detrimental if it leads to dependence on other countries, uneven development, exploitation, commercial rivalry leading to wars
Environmental concerns: global trade affecting environment, health and well-being; overuse of resources; need for sustainability
Free movement of goods but restricted movement of people (labour)
Ports: chief gateways of international trade; harbour vs port; docking, loading, unloading, storage facilities
Port quality measured by size of ships it can handle; ports serve hinterlands

Types of ports by type of traffic: industrial ports (bulk cargo - grain, sugar, ore, oil, chemicals), commercial ports (general cargo, packaged products, manufactured goods, passengers - e.g. Mumbai), comprehensive ports (bulk and general cargo in large volume - most major world ports)

Types of ports by location: inland ports (away from sea coast, linked via river or canal - Manchester, Memphis, Rhine ports Mannheim and Duisburg, Kolkata on Hooghly), out ports (deep water ports away from actual port serving parent port - Piraeus for Athens)

Types of ports by specialised functions: oil ports (tanker ports - Maracaibo in Venezuela, Esssahira in Tunisia, Abadan), ports of call (stopover ports for refuelling, watering, food - Aden, Honolulu, Singapore), packet station (ferry ports for passengers and mail across short distances - Dover and Calais across English Channel), entrepot ports (collection centres for re-export - Singapore for Asia, Rotterdam for Europe, Copenhagen for Baltic), naval ports (strategic ports for warships - Kochi, Karwar in India)
Map work: major seaports of the world
Exercise types: MCQs on trade blocs, ports, WTO; distinguish bilateral vs multilateral trade; explain balance of trade; basis of international trade; WTO functions and criticism; types of ports

chapters.title: India: Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition

concepts.text: India second most populous country after China; 1,210.8 million people in 2011 (about 17.5 percent of world population) on 2.4 percent of world area
Population as a resource and the pressure of large population on limited resources
Census of India: data collected every 10 years by Census of India; first census 1872, first complete census 1881
Census provides data on population distribution, density, growth, sex ratio, literacy, workers
Uneven distribution: Uttar Pradesh highest population, followed by Maharashtra, Bihar, West Bengal and Andhra Pradesh (together about half of population)
Rajasthan largest state by area has only 5.67 percent population
Low population in high altitude areas (Himalayas), arid regions (western Rajasthan), forest and tribal areas
Factors: physical (terrain, climate, water availability - North Indian plains, deltas, coastal plains have high population)
Socio-economic and historical factors: evolution of settled agriculture, transport network, industrialisation and urbanisation
Urban regions of Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, Bengaluru, Pune, Ahmedabad, Chennai, Jaipur attract migrants
Map reading: distribution of population in India
Density: number of persons per unit area; India 382 persons per sq km in 2011 (up from 117 in 1951)
Range: Arunachal Pradesh 17 persons per sq km to National Capital Territory of Delhi 11,297
High density states: Bihar (1,102), West Bengal (1,029), Uttar Pradesh (828); Kerala and Tamil Nadu relatively high in Peninsula
Low density: hilly, dissected, rugged terrain - Assam and north-eastern states except Assam, mountainous states like Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand
Physiological density: total population / net cultivated area
Agricultural density: total agricultural population / net cultivable area (agricultural population includes cultivators and agricultural labourers and their families)
Map work: states with highest and lowest density of population (2011)
Growth of population: change in number of people over time; absolute numbers and percentage
Natural growth (birth rate minus death rate) and induced growth (volume of in and out migration)
Annual growth rate of India about 1.64 percent in 2011
Phase I (1901-1921): stagnant or stationary phase; high birth and death rates; poor health, illiteracy, inefficient distribution of food
Phase II (1921-1951): steady population growth; improvements in health, sanitation, transport and communication; mortality decline

Phase III (1951-1981): period of population explosion; rapid fall in mortality and high fertility; developmental activities under Five Year Plans; international migration from Tibet, Bangladesh, Nepal, Pakistan
Phase IV (post-1981 till present): growth rate high but started slowing down gradually; declining birth rate due to rise in marriage age, improved quality of life, female education
Table/graph type: decadal growth rates of India 1901-2011; data interpretation
Growth rates varied between states: Kerala, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, Puducherry, Goa had low growth (below 20 percent) during 1991-2001
Kerala lowest decadal growth (9.4 percent) and Nagaland highest (64.5 percent) in 1991-2001
North-western, northern and north-central states (Punjab, Haryana, UP, Uttarakhand, Rajasthan, Bihar etc.) had relatively high growth
2001-2011 growth rates declined in most states compared with 1991-2001
Adolescent population (10-19 years) - about 20.9 percent of population in 2011; potential resource but vulnerable (early marriage, illiteracy, school dropout, malnutrition, drug abuse, HIV/AIDS)
National Youth Policy (2014): holistic development of youth; National Population Policy
Map reading: population growth rate by states
Population composition: age, sex, place of residence, ethnic characteristics, tribes, language, religion, marital status, literacy and education, occupation
Rural-urban composition: 68.8 percent rural and 31.2 percent urban in 2011; about 6,40,867 villages
Rural population distribution varies: Himachal Pradesh, Bihar highly rural; Goa, Maharashtra relatively urbanised
Urban population increase due to economic development, health and hygiene; concentration in large urban agglomerations
Linguistic composition: India a land of linguistic diversity (179 languages and 544 dialects per Grierson); 22 scheduled languages
Linguistic classification: Austric (Nishada), Dravidian (Dravida), Sino-Tibetan (Kirata), Indo-European (Aryan) families with sub-families, branches and speech areas
Religious composition: Hindus majority, Muslims largest minority, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains; spatial distribution of religious groups
Population divided into main workers (work at least 183 days a year), marginal workers (less than 183 days) and non-workers
Work participation rate in 2011 about 39.8 percent of population; higher in less developed areas
Occupational categories in Census: cultivators, agricultural labourers, household industrial workers, other workers
About 54.6 percent of total workers are cultivators and agricultural labourers; secondary and tertiary sectors smaller
Gender differences: female participation lower in all sectors; more women in primary sector

Spatial variation: high share of cultivators in Himachal Pradesh, Nagaland; agricultural labourers in Andhra Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Odisha; urbanised areas like Delhi, Chandigarh, Puducherry have more other workers
Exercise types: MCQs on census, density, phases of growth; physiological vs agricultural density; regional variation in growth; adolescent population challenges; occupational composition; map marking
Human settlement: cluster of dwellings of any type or size where human beings live; may be temporary or permanent
Settlements range from hamlets to metropolitan cities; size changes economic character and social structure
Rural settlements: smaller and sparsely located; primary activities (agriculture, fishing, forestry)
Urban settlements: generally compact, larger, engaged in non-primary (secondary and tertiary) activities
Rural people have intimate social relations; urban relations are formal; cities act as nodes of economic growth
Types determined by extent of built-up area and inter-house distance
Factors: nature of terrain, altitude, climate, availability of water; social structure, caste and religion; defence against thefts and robberies

Clustered, agglomerated or nucleated: compact, closely built-up houses separated from fields; common in fertile alluvial plains and north-eastern states; sometimes rectangular, radial, linear patterns
Bundelkhand region of central India and Nagaland: compact settlements for security; Rajasthan: scarcity of water leads to clustered settlements

Semi-clustered or fragmented: tendency of clustering in restricted area, or segregation of a large compact village; dominant community in central part, lower strata on periphery; widespread in Gujarat plains and parts of Rajasthan

Hamleted settlements: settlement fragmented into several units physically separated but sharing common name - panna, para, palli, nagla, dhani; middle and lower Ganga plain, Chhattisgarh, lower valleys of Himalayas

Dispersed or isolated settlements: isolated huts or hamlets of few huts in remote jungles, small hills with farms or pastures; extreme dispersion due to fragmented terrain and land resource base; Meghalaya, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh, Kerala
Activity type: identify types of rural settlements from pictures or maps
Urban centres: compact and larger; varied non-agricultural, economic and administrative functions
Cities functionally linked to rural areas: exchange of goods and services; directly or through market towns

Census definition of urban: places with municipality, corporation, cantonment board or notified town area committee; or minimum 5,000 population, at least 75 percent male workers in non-agricultural pursuits and density at least 400 persons per sq km
Towns flourished since prehistoric times: Harappa and Mohenjodaro
Ancient towns: over 2,000 years old; religious and cultural centres - Varanasi, Prayag (Allahabad), Pataliputra (Patna), Madurai
Medieval towns: about 100 headquarters of principalities and kingdoms; fort towns on ruins of ancient towns - Delhi, Hyderabad, Jaipur, Lucknow, Agra, Nagpur
Modern towns: developed by British and other Europeans; trading ports - Surat, Daman, Goa, Puducherry; British consolidated Mumbai (Bombay), Chennai (Madras), Kolkata (Calcutta) on western style
British introduced administrative centres, hill towns as summer resorts; civil, administrative and military areas

After 1850 modern industries led to towns like Jamshedpur; after independence administrative headquarters (Chandigarh, Bhubaneswar, Gandhinagar, Dispur) and industrial centres (Durgapur, Bhilai, Sindri, Barauni); satellite towns around metropolitan cities (Ghaziabad, Rohtak, Gurugram around Delhi)
Level of urbanisation measured as percentage of urban population to total population
Urbanisation in India 31.16 percent in 2011 - low compared to developed countries
Urban population increased eleven-fold during 20th century; enlargement of urban centres and emergence of new towns
Growth rate of urbanisation slowed during last two decades
Table/graph type: trends of urbanisation in India 1901-2011
Classification of towns on basis of population size: Census classifies urban centres into six classes; Class I - population over 100,000
Cities with 1-5 million population called metropolitan cities; more than 5 million - mega cities
Urban agglomeration: town and its adjoining urban outgrowths; two or more contiguous towns with or without outgrowths; city with one or more contiguous towns
Majority of metropolitan and mega cities are urban agglomerations; Greater Mumbai largest agglomeration, followed by Delhi, Kolkata, Chennai, Bengaluru
Smart Cities Mission: promote cities providing core infrastructure, clean and sustainable environment, decent quality of life using smart solutions
Towns classified on basis of dominant or specialised functions
Administrative towns and cities: administrative headquarters of higher order - Chandigarh, New Delhi, Bhopal, Shillong, Guwahati, Imphal, Srinagar, Gandhinagar, Jaipur, Chennai
Industrial towns: industries as prime motive force - Mumbai, Salem, Coimbatore, Modinagar, Jamshedpur, Hugli, Bhilai
Transport cities: ports engaged in export and import (Kandla, Kochchi, Kozhikode, Visakhapatnam) or hubs of inland transport (Agra, Dhulia, Mughal Sarai, Itarsi, Katni)
Commercial towns: trade and commerce - Kolkata, Saharanpur, Satna
Mining towns: mineral rich areas - Raniganj, Jharia, Digboi, Ankaleshwar, Singrauli
Garrison cantonment towns: Ambala, Jalandhar, Mhow, Babina, Udhampur
Educational towns: Roorkee, Varanasi, Aligarh, Pilani, Allahabad
Religious and cultural towns: Varanasi, Mathura, Amritsar, Madurai, Puri, Ajmer, Pushkar, Tirupati, Kurukshetra, Haridwar, Ujjain
Tourist towns: Nainital, Mussoorie, Shimla, Pachmarhi, Jodhpur, Jaisalmer, Udagamandalam (Ooty), Mount Abu
Cities are dynamic and their functions change over time; multi-functional cities

Exercise types: MCQs on settlement types and town functions; differentiate rural and urban settlements; factors of rural settlement types; evolution of towns; urban agglomeration; functional classification with examples
Land is basic resource; land use records maintained by land revenue department
Reporting area differs from geographical area (Survey of India measures geographical area); some areas unsurveyed
Nine land use categories in revenue records
Forests: area under actual forest cover differs from area classified as forest (demarcated by government)
Land put to non-agricultural uses: settlements, roads, canals, industries, shops
Barren and wastelands: hilly terrain, desert lands, ravines that cannot be brought under cultivation
Area under permanent pastures and grazing lands: owned by village panchayat or government; common property
Area under miscellaneous tree crops and groves (not included in net sown area): orchards and fruit trees owned privately
Culturable wasteland: land left fallow (uncultivated) for more than five years; can be reclaimed
Current fallow: land left without cultivation for one or less than one agricultural year; cultural practice to restore fertility
Fallow other than current fallow: cultivable land left uncultivated for more than one year but less than five years
Net area sown: physical extent of land on which crops are sown and harvested
Land-use changes depend on size of economy, composition of economy and pressure of population
Growth of economy increases pressure on land; marginal lands come under use
Composition of economy changes over time; secondary and tertiary sectors grow faster than agriculture; land shifts from agricultural to non-agricultural uses
Agricultural land remains under pressure as share of agriculture in GDP declines while dependence on it remains high
Increase in four categories (1950-51 to 2014-15): forest, non-agricultural uses, current fallow, net area sown
Decline in barren and wasteland, culturable wasteland, area under pastures and tree crops, fallow other than current fallow
Reasons: forest increase due to demarcation; non-agricultural uses due to urbanisation and industrialisation; declining wasteland due to agriculture expansion
Graph interpretation: changes in shares of land-use categories
Land classified as private property and common property resources (CPRs)
CPRs owned by state for use of community: fodder for livestock, fuel for households, forest products (fruits, nuts, fibre, medicinal plants)
In rural areas, CPRs are particularly important for landless and marginal farmers and women
Community forests, pasture lands, village water bodies and other public spaces as CPRs; need for protection by community
Land resources more crucial for agriculture-dependent population; quality of land affects agricultural productivity
Ownership of land has social value and security; landlessness and poverty link
Total stock of agricultural land: net sown area + all fallow lands + culturable wasteland
Net sown area about 54 percent of total reporting area in India; scope for expansion limited
Need to increase cropping intensity and productivity
Three distinct cropping seasons: kharif, rabi and zaid
Kharif: with south-west monsoon; tropical crops like rice, cotton, jute, jowar, bajra, tur
Rabi: with onset of winter in October-November, harvested March-April; wheat, gram, mustard
Zaid: short-duration summer season after rabi harvest; watermelons, cucumbers, vegetables and fodder crops on irrigated lands
Regional variation: no distinct seasons in southern parts; high temperature allows tropical crops year-round
Table: cropping seasons with major crops in northern and southern states
Classification by main source of moisture: irrigated and rainfed (barani) farming
Irrigated farming: protective irrigation (protect crops from soil moisture deficiency) vs productive irrigation (high productivity, higher water input)

Rainfed farming: dryland farming (rainfall below 75 cm; hardy crops like ragi, bajra, moong, gram, guar; moisture conservation) vs wetland farming (rainfall exceeds soil moisture requirement; rice, jute, sugarcane; aquaculture)
Map reading: irrigated area and rainfall map interpretation
Foodgrains dominate cropping; cereals and pulses
Cereals: fine grains (rice, wheat) and coarse grains (jowar, bajra, maize, ragi)
Rice: staple food; kharif crop in north, three crops (aus, aman, boro) in West Bengal; grown from humid tropics to hills; India second largest producer after China
Rice production: West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh, Punjab leading; high yields in Punjab, Tamil Nadu, Haryana, Andhra Pradesh, West Bengal, Kerala; rainfed in some regions
Wheat: second most important cereal; rabi crop in temperate zone; leading states Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Haryana, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan; high yields with irrigation
Jowar (sorghum): rainfed crop in semi-arid areas of central and southern India; Maharashtra largest producer; kharif in north, rabi in south
Bajra (pearl millet): hot and dry climate in north-western and western India; hardy crop resisting dry spells; Maharashtra, Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan, Haryana
Maize: food and fodder crop on poor soils in semi-arid climate; Madhya Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh
Map work: leading producing states of rice, wheat, cotton, jute, sugarcane, tea, coffee
Pulses: important source of protein; leguminous crops increase soil fertility by fixing nitrogen
Grown mainly on drylands of Deccan, central plateaus and north-western parts
Gram: subtropical crop, rainfed, rabi season in central, western and north-western India; Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, Karnataka
Tur (arhar or pigeon pea): second important pulse; drylands of central and southern India; Maharashtra about one-third production; low yields
Oilseeds produce edible oils; Malwa plateau, Marathwada, Gujarat, Rajasthan, Telangana, Rayalseema, Karnataka plateau
Groundnut: rainfed kharif crop of drylands; rabi in south; Gujarat, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka leading
Rapeseed and mustard: rabi crops in subtropical north-west and central India; sensitive to frost; Rajasthan about one-third production
Other oilseeds: soyabean (Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra) and sunflower (Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra)
Cotton: tropical crop; kharif in semi-arid areas; short staple (Indian) and long staple (American 'narma') varieties; Gujarat, Maharashtra, Telangana; north-west, west and south regions
India ranks among top cotton producers; needs clear sky during flowering
Jute: used for coarse cloth, bags, sacks; West Bengal about three-fourths production; also Bihar, Assam; lost foreign markets after partition and synthetic substitutes
Sugarcane: tropical crop under irrigation in sub-humid and humid climates; Uttar Pradesh about two-fifths production; also Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh

Tea: plantation crop as beverage; introduced by British in Brahmaputra valley (Assam) in 1840; well-drained soils in humid and sub-humid tropics; Assam, Darjeeling and Jalpaiguri (West Bengal), Nilgiris, Cardamom hills; India second largest producer
Coffee: tropical plantation crop; three varieties - arabica, robusta and liberica; India grows arabica in Western Ghats; Karnataka about two-thirds production, Kerala, Tamil Nadu
Agriculture important sector; about 53 percent population depends on it for livelihood (Census 2011 basis)
Strategy after independence: increase foodgrain production by switching from cash crops to food crops, intensification of cropping, extension of cultivated land
Intensive Agricultural District Programme (IADP) and Intensive Agricultural Area Programme (IAAP) in 1960s; HYV seeds of wheat (Mexico) and rice (Philippines)
Green Revolution: package technology (HYV seeds, chemical fertilisers, irrigation, pesticides); initially confined to irrigated areas of Punjab, Haryana, western UP, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu
1980s: Planning Commission focus on rainfed areas; agro-climatic planning in 1988; diversification of agriculture
Liberalisation and WTO (1990s): pressure of international competition
Growth of agricultural output and technology: increase in production and yields; expansion of irrigation (gross irrigated area); use of fertilisers and HYV seeds
Graph interpretation: production of foodgrains and major crops over time
Dependence on erratic monsoon: only about one-third cultivated area irrigated; droughts and floods
Low productivity: yields lower than world averages; pressure on land resources and labour productivity
Constraints of financial resources and indebtedness: inputs expensive; crop failures; farmers' indebtedness and distress
Lack of land reforms: unequal distribution of land; exploitation by landlords; land reforms not effectively implemented
Small farm size and fragmentation of landholdings: more than 60 percent holdings less than one hectare; uneconomic holdings
Lack of commercialisation: farmers grow crops for self-consumption; small farms cannot afford commercial crops
Vast underemployment: seasonal unemployment of about 4-8 months in agriculture
Degradation of cultivable land: salinisation, alkalinisation, waterlogging due to faulty irrigation; erosion; loss of soil fertility; excessive chemicals

Exercise types: MCQs on land-use categories, crops and seasons; differentiate current fallow vs culturable wasteland; CPR importance; dryland vs wetland farming; problems of Indian agriculture; Green Revolution impact; map marking of leading crop-producing states
Water is cyclic and renewable but quantity limited; rising demand and declining quality
India has about 2.45 percent of world surface area, 4 percent of water resources, about 16-17 percent of world population
Total annual precipitation about 4,000 cubic km; surface water and replenishable groundwater 1,869 cubic km
Only 60 percent usable; total utilisable water resource 1,122 cubic km
Four major sources: rivers, lakes, ponds and tanks
About 10,360 rivers and tributaries longer than 1.6 km; mean annual flow in all river basins about 1,869 cubic km
Only about 690 cubic km (32 percent) of surface water can be utilised due to topographical, hydrological constraints
Water flow depends on catchment size and rainfall; Ganga, Brahmaputra and Barak have large catchments; more than 60 percent of flow in these rivers
Peninsular rivers like Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri have much utilised flow; water stress in southern basins
Total replenishable groundwater about 432 cubic km
Ganga and Brahmaputra basins have about 46 percent of replenishable groundwater
Groundwater utilisation very high in north-western region and parts of south India (Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu)
Moderate utilisation in Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Tripura, Maharashtra; low in Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Kerala
Over-exploitation causing fall of groundwater table; need for sustainable use
India has indented coastline; lagoons and lakes in Kerala, Odisha and West Bengal
Water in these lagoons is brackish; used for fishing and irrigating certain varieties of paddy crops and coconut
India traditionally agrarian; about two-thirds population depends on agriculture
Agriculture uses about 89 percent of surface water and 92 percent of groundwater utilisation
Industrial sector uses 2 percent of surface water and 5 percent of groundwater; domestic sector 9 percent of surface water (higher than groundwater)
Future demand from industrial and domestic sectors to increase
Demand of water for irrigation: rainfall uneven in space and time; dry season needs; multiple cropping needs irrigation; HYV crops need regulated moisture
Irrigation enhances productivity; Punjab, Haryana and western UP over 85 percent net sown area under irrigation; wheat and rice depend on irrigation
Problem of excessive irrigation: over-drawing of groundwater; increase in fluoride (Rajasthan, Maharashtra) and arsenic (West Bengal, Bihar) concentrations; soil salinity
Graph/pie type: sectoral usage of surface and groundwater
Per capita availability of water declining due to population increase
Deterioration of water quality: pollution by industrial, domestic and agricultural effluents with foreign matter
Polluted rivers: Ganga and Yamuna (examples of polluted stretches near Delhi, Kanpur, Varanasi)
Toxic substances enter lakes, streams, rivers, oceans and groundwater; contamination affects aquatic life and human health
Declining availability and rising demand require conservation and effective management
Strategies: water-saving technologies, prevention of pollution, watershed development, rainwater harvesting, water recycling and reuse, conjunctive use of water
Prevention of water pollution: Central Pollution Control Board monitoring; Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1974 and Environment Protection Act 1986 not effectively implemented
Recycle and reuse: use of treated water for industry (cooling, fire-fighting); waste water for gardening; reduce freshwater demand in urban areas
Watershed management: efficient management and conservation of surface and groundwater; preventing runoff, storage and recharge through percolation tanks, recharge wells

Watershed programmes: Haryali (central government, rural drinking water, irrigation, pisciculture, afforestation through gram panchayats), Neeru-Meeru (Water and You) in Andhra Pradesh, Arvary Pani Sansad in Alwar (Rajasthan)
Rainwater harvesting: capturing and storing rainwater for various uses; recharge aquifers; low-cost eco-friendly; traditional practices (lakes, ponds, kunds in Rajasthan)

Benefits of rainwater harvesting: increases water availability, checks declining groundwater table, improves quality by diluting fluoride and nitrate, prevents soil erosion and floods, arrests saline intrusion
Example: Ralegan Siddhi (Maharashtra) and Tamil Nadu mandatory rooftop rainwater harvesting
National Water Policy (2002) priorities: drinking water first, then irrigation, hydropower, navigation, industrial and other uses
Jal Kranti Abhiyan (2015-16): ensure water security through per capita water availability; Jal Gram (water-scarce villages) and model command areas; Jal Shakti approaches
Exercise types: MCQs on water resource figures and programmes; why water resources are declining; sectoral use; emerging problems; watershed management; rainwater harvesting methods and benefits
India rich in mineral resources due to varied geological structure; most valuable minerals pre-Palaeozoic in igneous and metamorphic rocks of Peninsula
Mineral: natural substance of organic or inorganic origin with definite chemical and physical properties
Characteristics of minerals: unevenly distributed; inverse relation between quality and quantity (good quality minerals are less in quantity); exhaustible and take long to replenish
Minerals as base for industrial development
Metallic minerals: ferrous (iron ore, manganese, chromite) and non-ferrous (copper, bauxite, lead, zinc, gold)
Non-metallic minerals: organic (fossil fuels - coal, petroleum) and inorganic (mica, limestone, graphite)
Diagram/flowchart: classification of minerals
Most metallic minerals in old crystalline rocks of Peninsular plateau; over 97 percent coal reserves in Damodar, Sone, Mahanadi and Godavari valleys
Petroleum reserves in sedimentary basins of Assam, Gujarat and Mumbai High (offshore Arabian Sea); new reserves in Krishna-Godavari and Kaveri basins
Three broad mineral belts: North-eastern Plateau region (Chotanagpur, Odisha plateau, West Bengal, Chhattisgarh) - iron ore, coal, manganese, bauxite, mica

South-western Plateau region (Karnataka, Goa, contiguous Tamil Nadu uplands, Kerala) - ferrous metals and bauxite, high-grade iron ore, manganese, limestone; Neyveli lignite; monazite sands of Kerala; Kolar gold mines
North-western region (Aravali in Rajasthan, Gujarat) - non-ferrous: copper, zinc; building stones (sandstone, granite, marble), gypsum, Fuller's earth; dolomite, limestone; Gujarat petroleum; salt
Himalayan belt: copper, lead, zinc, cobalt, tungsten; Assam valley mineral oil; offshore areas
Map reading: mineral belts of India
Iron ore: India has large reserves (about 20 percent of world); haematite and magnetite types
Iron ore mines close to coal fields in north-eastern plateau region
Odisha: Sundergarh, Mayurbhanj, Jhar (Gurumahisani, Sulaipet, Badampahar, Kiruburu, Bonai); Jharkhand: Noamundi, Gua (Poorbi and Paschimi Singhbhum)
Chhattisgarh: Dalli and Rajhara (Durg), Bailadila (Dantewara); Karnataka: Sandur-Hospet (Ballari), Baba Budan hills, Kudremukh (Chikkamagaluru); Maharashtra, Telangana, Goa
Manganese: important raw material for smelting iron ore and ferro alloys; found in Dharwar system

Odisha leading producer (Bonai, Kendujhar, Sundergarh, Gangpur, Koraput, Kalahandi, Bolangir); Karnataka (Dharwar, Ballari, Belagavi, Shivamogga, Chitradurga, Tumakuru); Maharashtra (Nagpur, Bhandara, Ratnagiri); Madhya Pradesh (Balaghat-Chhindwara-Nimar-Mandla-Jhabua belt); Telangana, Goa, Jharkhand
Map work: iron ore mines (Mayurbhanj, Durg, Bailadila, Ballari, Kudremukh)
India poorly endowed with non-ferrous metallic minerals except bauxite
Bauxite: ore for aluminium; found in tertiary deposits associated with laterite rocks in plateaus or hill ranges of Peninsula and coastal tracts

Bauxite distribution: Odisha largest producer (Kalahandi, Sambalpur, Bolangir, Koraput), Jharkhand (Lohardaga - patlands), Gujarat, Chhattisgarh (Amarkantak plateau), Madhya Pradesh (Katni-Jabalpur, Balaghat), Maharashtra (Kolaba, Thane, Ratnagiri, Satara, Pune, Kolhapur), Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Goa
Copper: used in electrical industry (wires, motors, transformers, generators); alloyable, malleable and ductile; jewellery
Copper deposits: Singhbhum district (Jharkhand), Balaghat (Madhya Pradesh), Jhunjhunu and Alwar (Rajasthan), Agnigundala (Andhra Pradesh), Chitradurg and Hasan (Karnataka), South Arcot (Tamil Nadu)
Map work: copper mines (Hazaribagh, Singhbhum, Khetri) and bauxite mines (Katni, Bilaspur, Koraput)
Mica: used in electrical and electronic industries; split into thin sheets; tough and flexible
Mica found in Hazaribagh plateau (Jharkhand), Nellore (Andhra Pradesh), Rajasthan (Jaipur-Bhilwara, Udaipur), Karnataka (Mysuru, Hasan), Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra, West Bengal
Map work: mica mines (Ajmer, Beawar, Nellore, Gaya, Hazaribagh)
Other non-metallic minerals: limestone, dolomite, phosphate
Mineral fuels essential for generation of power for agriculture, industry, transport
Coal: used in thermal power generation and smelting of iron ore
Two main geological ages: Gondwana coal (about 200 million years old; 80 percent of reserves) and tertiary coal (about 55 million years old)
Gondwana coalfields: Damodar valley (Jharkhand-Bengal coal belt: Raniganj, Jharia, Bokaro, Giridih, Karanpura); Jharia largest, followed by Raniganj

Other Gondwana fields: Godavari, Mahanadi, Son and Wardha valleys; Singrauli (MP-UP), Korba (Chhattisgarh), Talcher and Rampur (Odisha), Chanda-Wardha, Kamptee, Bander (Maharashtra), Singareni (Telangana), Pandur (Andhra Pradesh)
Tertiary coal in Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya and Nagaland (Darangiri, Cherrapunji, Mewlong, Langrin, Makum, Jaipur, Nazira, Namchik-Namphuk)
Lignite (brown coal) in coastal areas of Tamil Nadu (Neyveli), Puducherry, Gujarat, Jammu and Kashmir
Map work: coal mines (Jharia, Bokaro, Raniganj, Neyveli)
Crude petroleum: hydrocarbons in liquid and gaseous states; found in sedimentary rocks of Tertiary age
Petroleum essential for transport, industry, raw material for petrochemicals (fertilisers, synthetic rubber, synthetic fibre, medicines, vaseline, lubricants, wax, soap, cosmetics) - 'liquid gold'
Exploration began in 1956 after ONGC (Oil and Natural Gas Commission) set up; Digboi in Assam earliest (1889)
