Oil fields: Assam (Digboi, Naharkatiya, Moran), Gujarat (Ankaleshwar, Kalol, Mehsana, Nawagam, Kosamba, Lunej), Mumbai High (offshore, 1973 discovery), Krishna-Godavari and Kaveri basins
Refineries: field-based (Digboi) and market-based (Barauni); India's major refineries
Natural gas: Gas Authority of India Limited (GAIL, 1984) to transport and market natural gas; reserves in Tripura, Rajasthan, Gujarat, KG basin, offshore wells
Map work: oil refineries (Mathura, Jamnagar, Barauni) and oil fields (Digboi, Ankleshwar, Mumbai High)
Uranium and thorium as main nuclear minerals
Uranium deposits in Dharwar rocks: Singhbhum copper belt (Jaduguda in Jharkhand), Udaipur, Alwar, Jhunjhunu (Rajasthan), Durg (Chhattisgarh), Bhandara (Maharashtra), Kullu (Himachal Pradesh)

Thorium mainly from monazite and ilmenite in beach sands along Kerala and Tamil Nadu coast; Palakkad and Kollam districts of Kerala (world's richest monazite deposits); Visakhapatnam (Andhra Pradesh), Mahanadi delta (Odisha)
Atomic Energy Commission (1948); Atomic Energy Institute at Trombay (1954), renamed Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (1967)
Nuclear power projects: Tarapur (Maharashtra), Rawatbhata near Kota (Rajasthan), Kalpakkam (Tamil Nadu), Narora (Uttar Pradesh), Kaiga (Karnataka), Kakrapara (Gujarat)
Map work: nuclear power plants
Fossil fuels are exhaustible and cause pollution; non-conventional sources (solar, wind, hydro-geothermal, biomass) are renewable, equitably distributed and environment-friendly
Solar energy: photovoltaic and solar thermal technology; western parts of India (Gujarat, Rajasthan) have high potential; cost-effective and eco-friendly; used in heaters, dryers, cookers

Wind energy: absolutely pollution free, inexhaustible; kinetic energy of wind converted to electricity through turbines; Rajasthan, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Karnataka favourable; land and sea breezes and monsoon winds
Tidal and wave energy: ocean currents and waves; large potential along west coast; Gulf of Kachchh and Gulf of Khambhat; not yet utilised
Geothermal energy: heat from earth's interior via hot springs; Manikaran in Himachal Pradesh (first project); Puga valley in Ladakh

Bio-energy: energy derived from biological products - agricultural residues, municipal, industrial and other wastes; electricity, heat energy, gas for cooking; e.g. Okhla in Delhi waste-to-energy; improves rural economy, reduces environmental pollution
Sustainable development requires conservation of minerals and energy for future generations
Alternative energy sources (solar, wind, wave, geothermal) to replace exhaustible ones
Use of scrap metals and recycling; substitutes for scarce metals; reducing consumption
Export of strategic and scarce minerals must be reduced; improve mining techniques to reduce wastage

Exercise types: MCQs on mineral regions and fuels; classification of minerals; distribution of iron ore, manganese, bauxite, coal, petroleum; importance of non-conventional energy; conservation measures; map marking of mines and refineries

chapters.title: India: Planning and Sustainable Development in Indian Context

concepts.text: Planning: process of thinking, formulating a scheme or programme and implementing a set of actions to achieve a goal
Planning in India through Five Year Plans by Planning Commission (1950); First Plan 1951
Two approaches: sectoral planning (agriculture, irrigation, manufacturing, power, construction, transport, communication, social infrastructure) and regional planning
Regional planning to reduce regional imbalances in development; not uniform development across regions

NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India) replaced Planning Commission on 1 January 2015; think tank providing strategic and technical advice; bottom-up decentralised planning, cooperative federalism
Planning Commission introduced target area and target group approaches to arrest regional and social disparities
Target area programmes: Command Area Development Programme, Drought Prone Area Programme, Desert Development Programme, Hill Area Development Programme
Target group programmes: Small Farmers Development Agency (SFDA), Marginal Farmers Development Agency (MFDA)
Eighth Five Year Plan: special area programmes for infrastructure in hill areas, north-eastern states, tribal areas and backward areas

Initiated during Fifth Five Year Plan covering 15 districts in hilly districts of Uttar Pradesh (now Uttarakhand), Mikir hill and North Cachar hills of Assam, Darjeeling district of West Bengal and Nilgiri district of Tamil Nadu
National Committee on Development of Backward Areas (1981) recommended all hill areas above 600 m and not covered under tribal sub-plan be treated as backward hill areas
Plans to harness indigenous resources: horticulture, plantation agriculture, animal husbandry, poultry, forestry, small-scale and village industries
Consideration of local topography, ecology, social and economic conditions
Initiated during Fourth Five Year Plan to provide employment to people in drought-prone areas and create productive assets

Initially emphasised labour-intensive civil works; later emphasis on irrigation projects, land development, afforestation, grassland development, infrastructure (electricity, roads, market, credit, services)
National Committee on Development of Backward Areas noted it was confined to agriculture and allied sectors; restoration of ecological balance
Integrated watershed development approach; growing population pressure on marginal lands
Drought-prone areas identified by Planning Commission (1967): 67 districts, Irrigation Commission (1972) criterion of 30 percent irrigated area

Drought-prone areas: Rajasthan, Gujarat, western Madhya Pradesh, Marathwada, Rayalseema and Telangana plateaus, Karnataka plateau, highlands and interior of Tamil Nadu; also some districts of Punjab, Haryana, northern Rajasthan (spared by irrigation)

sections.name: 14.5 Case study: Integrated Tribal Development Project in Bharmaur region

concepts.text: Bharmaur tribal area: Bharmaur and Holi tehsils of Chamba district, Himachal Pradesh; notified tribal area since 21 November 1975
Inhabited by Gaddis, a tribal community with distinct identity in Himalayan region; transhumance; Gaddiali dialect
Geography: harsh climate, low resource base, fragile environment; Ravi and its tributaries Budhil and Tundahen; Dhaula Dhar and Pir Panjal ranges
Climate: sub-freezing in winter, snowfall; mild in summer; Gaddis migrate to lower areas in winter
Economy based on agriculture and allied activities like sheep and goat rearing; economic backwardness and isolation
Tribal sub-plan introduced in 1974 during Fifth Five Year Plan; Bharmaur designated one of five Integrated Tribal Development Projects (ITDP) in Himachal Pradesh
Aim: improve quality of life of Gaddis and narrow gap between Bharmaur and other areas of HP; priority to transport and communication, agriculture and allied activities, social and community services
Outcomes: development of schools, healthcare facilities, potable water, roads, communications, electricity

Benefits from Ravi river region: Holi and Khani areas benefited most; increase in literacy rate (female literacy from 1.88 percent in 1971 to 65 percent in 2011), improved sex ratio and decline in child marriage
Shift from traditional crops to pulses and cash crops; less transhumance; more people engaged in secondary and tertiary sectors
Map reading: Bharmaur tribal region location
Development concept changed: earlier economic growth; later social welfare and qualitative change
Late 1960s: environmental awareness in western world; 'The Population Bomb' by Ehrlich (1968) and 'The Limits to Growth' by Meadows et al. (1972)
UN established World Commission on Environment and Development (WCED) headed by Gro Harlem Brundtland; report 'Our Common Future' (1987, Brundtland Report)
Definition: development that meets needs of present without compromising ability of future generations to meet their own needs
Sustainable development integrates ecological, social and economic aspects; Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) adopted by UN

sections.name: 14.7 Case study: Indira Gandhi Canal command area

concepts.text: Indira Gandhi Canal (Rajasthan Canal): one of the largest canal systems in India; conceived by Kanwar Sain in 1948; launched 31 March 1958
Originates at Harike barrage in Punjab; runs parallel to Pakistan border at average distance of 40 km in Thar desert (Marusthali) of Rajasthan
Total planned length 9,060 km; culturable command area of 19.6 lakh hectares; 70 percent area under flow irrigation, rest lift irrigation

Construction in two stages: Stage-I command area in Ganganagar, Hanumangarh and northern Bikaner districts (gently undulating topography; 5.53 lakh hectares, 1960s); Stage-II in Bikaner, Jaisalmer, Barmer, Jodhpur, Nagaur and Churu districts (14.10 lakh hectares, shifting dunes, desert; temperature above 50 degrees C in summer)
Lift canals in stage-II command area lift water up against slope
Positive impacts: soil moisture availability increased; afforestation and pasture development; reduced soil erosion and wind erosion; canal water also for drinking
Agricultural changes: increase in cultivated area and intensity of cropping; traditional crops (gram, bajra, guar) replaced by wheat, cotton, groundnut and rice
Negative impacts: intensive irrigation and excessive water use leading to waterlogging and soil salinity; long-term sustainability concerns
Map reading: Indira Gandhi Canal command area

sections.name: 14.8 Measures for promotion of sustainable development

concepts.text: Strict implementation of water management policy; protective irrigation in stage I, extensive irrigation of crops and pasture in stage II
Cropping pattern should not include water-intensive crops; plantation crops like citrus fruits instead of rice
Command area development programmes: lining of watercourses, land development and levelling, warabandi system (equal distribution of canal water in command area)
Reclaim areas affected by waterlogging and soil salinity
Eco-development through afforestation, shelterbelt plantation and pasture development, especially in fragile stage-II
Provide adequate financial and institutional support to poor landholders for cultivation of land allotted
Development of other sectors (agro-processing, marketing) to diversify economy beyond agriculture

Exercise types: MCQs on DPAP, ITDP, IGNP; differentiate sectoral and regional planning; target area planning; hill area development; Bharmaur outcomes; sustainable development concept; measures for sustainable development in IGNP command area
Transport and communication as lifelines of economy; movement of goods, services and ideas
Means of transport and communication evolved from ancient routes (Grand Trunk road, Silk route) to modern networks
Modes: land (road, rail), water, air, pipelines; communication (personal and mass)
Pathways and unmetalled roads used since ancient times; modern roads with economic and technological development
Sher Shah Suri built Shahi (royal) road from Sonargaon (Bangladesh) to Peshawar; renamed Grand Trunk (GT) road by British (Kolkata to Peshawar), now Amritsar to Kolkata
India has one of largest road networks in world (about 62 lakh km); about 85 percent passenger and 70 percent freight traffic by road
Road development: Nagpur Plan (1943), twenty-year road plan (1961)
Classification of roads: national highways, state highways, district roads, rural roads, other roads (border roads, international highways)
National Highways: constructed and maintained by central government; for inter-state transport and strategic movement; about 2 percent of road length but 40 percent of road traffic

National Highways Authority of India (NHAI, 1995): autonomous body under Ministry of Road Transport and Highways; Golden Quadrilateral linking Delhi-Mumbai-Chennai-Kolkata; North-South corridor (Srinagar to Kanyakumari) and East-West corridor (Silchar to Porbandar)
State Highways: constructed and maintained by state governments; join state capitals with district headquarters
District roads: connect district headquarters with other important nodes; maintained by Zila Parishad
Rural roads: vital for rural areas; Pradhan Mantri Grameen Sadak Yojana (PMGSY) for all-weather road connectivity to villages
Other roads: Border Roads Organisation (BRO, 1960) constructs strategic roads in difficult terrain (e.g. Chandigarh-Manali-Leh road); international highways linking neighbouring countries
Distribution of roads: road density highest in Kerala, lowest in Jammu and Kashmir/Ladakh; uneven due to terrain and economic development
Map reading: national highways network and Golden Quadrilateral
Indian Railways: major mode for long-distance freight and passengers; first train from Mumbai to Thane in 1853 (34 km)
One of largest government undertakings; network of about 67,000+ km; 17-18 zones
Gauges: broad gauge (1.676 m), metre gauge (1 m), narrow gauge (0.762 m and 0.610 m); Project Unigauge to convert metre and narrow gauge to broad gauge
Metro rail services in Kolkata (first, 1984), Delhi and other cities; steam engines replaced by diesel and electric

Konkan Railway (1998): 760 km from Roha (Maharashtra) to Mangaluru (Karnataka); engineering marvel - 146 rivers, 2,000 bridges, 73 tunnels; Asia's largest tunnel (6.5 km); Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka partner states
Railways promote tourism (Palace on Wheels, Darjeeling Himalayan Railway, Nilgiri Mountain Railway); Dedicated Freight Corridors
Water transport cheapest for heavy and bulky goods; fuel-efficient and eco-friendly
Inland waterways: rivers, canals, backwaters, creeks; 14,500 km navigable waterways; Inland Waterways Authority (1986)
National Waterway 1: Ganga between Allahabad (Prayagraj) and Haldia (1,620 km)
National Waterway 2: Brahmaputra between Sadiya and Dhubri (891 km)
National Waterway 3: West Coast Canal from Kottapuram to Kollam, Udyogamandal and Champakkara canals (205 km)
Other National Waterways: NW4 (Kakinada-Puducherry with Godavari-Krishna), NW5 (Brahmani, East Coast Canal, Mahanadi delta); 111 waterways declared national waterways (2016)
Oceanic routes: India's long coastline of 7,517 km with 12 major and about 200 minor ports; about 95 percent of foreign trade by volume and 70 percent by value moves through oceanic routes
Fastest, most comfortable and prestigious mode; covers difficult terrain
Air transport began in 1911 with airmail between Allahabad and Naini (10 km); Airport Authority of India
Air India: international air services; nationalisation in 1953 and recent privatisation; Indian Airlines merged
Pawan Hans Helicopters Ltd: helicopter services to ONGC offshore, inaccessible areas and difficult terrains like north-eastern states, interiors of J and K, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand
UDAN (Ude Desh ka Aam Nagrik) regional connectivity scheme
Map reading: international and domestic airports
Pipelines most convenient and efficient for liquids and gases over long distances; also solids converted to slurry

Oil India Limited (OIL): exploration, production and transportation of crude oil and natural gas; first cross-country pipeline from Naharkatiya oilfield to Barauni refinery (1,157 km), extended to Kanpur
Salaya-Koyali-Mathura pipeline from Gujarat to Mathura via Viramgram, Chaksu; branch to Panipat
Gas Authority of India Limited (GAIL, 1984): HVJ (Hazira-Vijaipur-Jagdishpur) gas pipeline connecting Mumbai High and Bassein gas fields with fertiliser, power and industrial complexes
Advantages of pipelines; reduces transport by road and rail; Indian Oil's pipeline network
Communication: exchange of messages from earlier drum beats and messengers to modern telecommunications
Personal communication system: Postal service (largest in world), telegraph, telephone, mobile phones, internet
Internet: e-mail, e-commerce; used in urban areas mostly; Digital India initiative
Telecommunication: India's mobile phone network among largest in world; Subscriber Trunk Dialling (STD), fibre optics
Mass communication: radio (All India Radio / Akashvani, 1923/1936), television (Doordarshan since 1959; national broadcaster; one of largest terrestrial networks)
Press: newspapers in many languages; Hindi newspapers largest number; Films: India largest producer of feature films, documentaries; Central Board of Film Certification

Satellite communication: India's satellite systems - INSAT (Indian National Satellite System, 1983) for telecommunications, meteorological observation and broadcasting; IRS (Indian Remote Sensing Satellite System, 1988) for resource monitoring
National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC) at Hyderabad; data used for resource management; ISRO

Exercise types: MCQs on roads, railways, waterways, pipelines; importance of National Highways and BRO; Konkan Railway significance; national waterways; role of satellite communication; mass communication; differences between road and rail transport
International trade: exchange of goods and services among countries; no country is self-sufficient
India's share in world trade about 1 percent; integral part of world economy
Exports and imports; balance of trade concept recap

sections.name: 16.2 Changing pattern of India's international trade

concepts.text: Volume of trade increased from Rs 1,214 crore in 1950-51 to about Rs 77,19,796 crore in 2020-21
Reasons for growth: momentum in manufacturing sectors, liberal government policies, diversification of markets
Imports have consistently exceeded exports; increasing trade deficit (negative balance of trade)
Reasons for deficit: price rise in crude petroleum on international market; rising imports of gold, electronics, machinery
Foreign trade policy and liberalisation (1991) boosted trade
Table/graph type: India's exports, imports and trade balance over years

sections.name: 16.3 Changing pattern of composition of India's exports

concepts.text: Decline in share of agriculture and allied products (coffee, spices, tea, pulses) due to international competition
Increase in share of petroleum and crude products (due to rising petroleum prices and refining capacity), and other commodities
Rise in share of manufactured goods: over 67-75 percent of exports; engineering goods with significant growth; gems and jewellery a large share
Rise in exports of floricultural products, fresh fruits, marine products and sugar
Competition from China and East Asian countries in manufacturing
Table type: composition of exports (percentage share of commodity groups)

sections.name: 16.4 Changing pattern of composition of India's imports

concepts.text: 1950s-1960s: imports dominated by foodgrains, capital goods, machinery and equipment due to food shortage
After Green Revolution in 1970s, foodgrain imports discontinued; replaced by fertilisers and petroleum
Machinery and equipment, special steel, edible oil, chemicals make up import basket
Large increase in petroleum and its products imports - used as fuel and industrial raw material; reflects industrialisation and rising standard of living
Other imports: pearls and precious stones, gold and silver, metallic ores, metal scrap, non-ferrous metals, electronic goods
Table type: composition of imports (percentage share)
India has trade relations with most countries and major trading blocs of world
Regions: Asia and ASEAN, Europe, America, Africa, CIS and Baltic, Latin America
India aims to double share in international trade; promotion of exports
Major trading partners: USA, China, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Hong Kong, Switzerland, Germany, Singapore, Belgium, UK
Changing pattern: Asia and Oceania growing share; decreasing share of Europe
Table type: direction of India's trade by regions

sections.name: 16.6 Sea ports as gateways of international trade

concepts.text: India surrounded by sea on three sides; ports as gateways; 95 percent of trade by volume moves through sea
Coastline of 7,517 km; 12 major ports and about 200 minor or intermediate ports
Major ports controlled by central government; minor ports by state governments
Ports developed under British influence as suction points for resources; Kolkata, Mumbai, Chennai earliest
Partition led to loss of Karachi port; Kandla port developed on west and Diamond Harbour near Kolkata
Deendayal (Kandla) port: Gulf of Kachchh; developed to reduce pressure on Mumbai after partition; tidal port; handles petroleum, fertilisers; Vadinar offshore terminal
Mumbai port: natural harbour and biggest port; close to Middle East, Mediterranean, North Africa, North America, Europe; large hinterland - Maharashtra, Gujarat, MP, Rajasthan, Delhi
Jawaharlal Nehru Port (Nhava Sheva): developed as satellite port to relieve Mumbai pressure; largest container port in India
Marmagao port: entrance of Zuari estuary, Goa; natural harbour; handles iron ore exports (about 50 percent of India's iron ore export); Konkan railway increased hinterland
New Mangalore port: Karnataka; exports iron ore and iron concentrates from Kudremukh; fertilisers, petroleum products, edible oils, coffee, tea
Kochchi port: head of Vembanad Kayal (Queen of Arabian Sea); natural harbour; close to Suez-Colombo route; caters to Kerala, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu
Kolkata port: on Hugli river, 128 km inland from Bay of Bengal; riverine port; requires dredging; serves large hinterland of Ganga-Brahmaputra basin; competition from neighbouring ports
Haldia port: 105 km downstream of Kolkata; developed to reduce congestion on Kolkata port; bulk cargo - iron ore, coal, petroleum, fertilisers, jute, cotton
Paradip port: Mahanadi delta, Odisha (about 100 km from Cuttack); deepest harbour; handles large vessels; exports iron ore; hinterland Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand
Visakhapatnam port: Andhra Pradesh; landlocked harbour connected to sea by channel cut through solid rock and sand; iron ore exports; petroleum and general cargo; outer harbour
Chennai port: one of oldest ports on east coast; artificial harbour built in 1859; not suitable for large ships due to shallow waters near coast; hinterland Tamil Nadu, Puducherry
Ennore (Kamarajar) port: newly developed 25 km north of Chennai to relieve pressure
V.O. Chidambaranar (Tuticorin) port: Tamil Nadu; natural harbour and rich hinterland; coal, salt, foodgrains, edible oils, sugar, chemicals and petroleum products; trade with Sri Lanka, Maldives
Map work: major seaports of India
Air transport plays important role in international trade: carries high-value or perishable goods, reduces time
Air transport costly; unsuitable for heavy and bulky commodities; low share in international trade
Major international airports: Ahmedabad, Bengaluru, Chennai, Delhi, Goa, Hyderabad, Kolkata, Mumbai, Thiruvananthapuram, Amritsar, Guwahati, Kochi, Srinagar etc.
Map work: major international airports of India
Exercise types: MCQs on ports, trading partners, imports; changes in composition of exports and imports; trade deficit causes; ports as gateways; features of major ports; role of air transport

chapters.title: India: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems

concepts.text: Environmental pollution: release of substances and energy as waste products of human activities causing harmful effects on natural environment
Types of pollution based on medium: air, water, land and noise pollution
Pollutants classified by origin and transport; pollutants move through air, water and soil
Indiscriminate use of water by growing population and industrial expansion has degraded water quality
Natural sources of pollution (erosion, landslides, decay of plants and animals) and human sources (industrial, agricultural, cultural activities)
Industrial pollutants: industrial wastes, polluted waste water, poisonous gases, chemical residues, heavy metals, dust, smoke; industries - leather, pulp and paper, textiles and chemicals
Agricultural sources: inorganic fertilisers, pesticides, herbicides seep into groundwater and surface water
Cultural activities: pilgrimage, religious fairs, tourism cause water pollution; immersion of idols, bathing
Health effects: water-borne diseases - diarrhoea, intestinal worms, hepatitis; about one-fourth of communicable diseases are water-borne
Case studies: Ganga polluted stretches (Kanpur, Allahabad, Varanasi, Patna, Kolkata) and Yamuna (Delhi, Agra, Mathura)
Namami Gange Programme (2014) under National Mission for Clean Ganga: sewerage treatment, river front development, river surface cleaning, afforestation, industrial effluent monitoring, Ganga Gram
Activity type: identify sources of water pollution in local river/pond
Air pollution: addition of contaminants (dust, fumes, gas, fog, odour, smoke, vapour) in substantial proportion and duration harmful to flora, fauna and property
Sources: combustion of fossil fuels, mining, industries; oxides of sulphur and nitrogen, hydrocarbons, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, lead and asbestos
Effects: diseases of respiratory, nervous and circulatory systems
Urban smog caused by atmospheric pollution; acid rain
Air quality: industrial cities (e.g. Delhi) with high levels of air pollution; National Clean Air Programme
Noise pollution: state of unbearable and uncomfortable noise caused by various sources
Sources: factories, mechanised construction and demolition, automobiles, aircraft, sirens, loudspeakers, festivals
Measured in decibels (dB); traffic noise most significant; levels vary with types of vehicles
Effects: hearing impairment, stress, sleep disturbance; noise pollution location-specific - more in urban areas, industrial areas, transport routes
Activity type: survey noise levels at different locations
Overcrowding, congestion, inadequate facilities and poor sanitation cause serious environmental and health problems in Indian cities
Solid wastes from households (personal and domestic waste) and industrial/commercial establishments
Problems: foul smell, flies and rodents, breeding of disease vectors (typhoid, diphtheria, diarrhoea, malaria, cholera); wastes blown by wind and spread in rain
Industrial waste dumped into rivers; untreated sewage leads to river pollution
Large share of urban waste remains uncollected; need for collection and management
Solutions: waste as resource for energy and compost; recycling, segregation at source; Swachh Bharat Mission
Flow of population from rural to urban areas due to high demand of labour in cities, low job opportunities and low wages in rural areas
Migrants generally unskilled or semi-skilled; settle in slums; pressure on urban infrastructure
Male-selective migration from rural areas; families left behind; women burden
Case study narrative: Ramesh, a migrant welder from rural area, illustrates push and pull factors, informal employment, and remittances to family
Indian cities show dual society: well-developed planned colonies vs slums, jhuggi-jhopri clusters, shanty towns
Slums: residential areas least preferred, dilapidated houses, poor hygiene, poor ventilation, lack of basic amenities (drinking water, light, toilets)
Slum dwellers: overcrowded, narrow lanes, fire hazards; poverty, malnutrition, illness; vulnerable to drug abuse, alcoholism, crime, social exclusion
Most slum dwellers work in low-paid, high-risk informal sector jobs
Case study: Dharavi (Mumbai) - Asia's one of largest slums; narrow lanes, congested houses, no drainage, poor sanitation; yet large informal economy (pottery, leather, recycling)
Urban renewal and slum rehabilitation schemes
Land degradation: temporary or permanent decline in productive capacity of land due to natural and human causes
Pressure on agricultural land increased by limited availability; wasteland as degraded land
Natural processes of degradation: gullied/ravinous land, desertic or coastal sands, barren rocky areas, steep sloping land, glacial areas
Human-induced degradation: waterlogged and marshy areas, land affected by salinity and alkalinity, degraded forest and grazing land, mining and industrial wasteland
Measures: afforestation, check dams, soil conservation, controlled grazing, watershed management
